own_scenes.desc: En septiembre de 1964 las autoridades de la Universidad de California intentaron prohibir los mítines por los derechos civiles; la sentada que siguió, con la retórica de Mario Savio («poned vuestros cuerpos sobre los engranajes»), se convirtió en el Free Speech Movement. En mayo de 1965 Jerry Rubin y Abbie Hoffman, entre otros, fundaron el Vietnam Day Committee, que piqueteó los trenes de tropas de Oakland bajo el lema «Make Love Not War». Hubo marcha del SDS y el SNCC en Washington, quema de cartillas de reclutamiento (castigada desde agosto de 1965 con cinco años de cárcel) y grandes manifestaciones el 15 de octubre. De ese fermento salió «I Feel Like I’m Fixin’ to Die Rag» de Country Joe McDonald (Rag Baby, octubre de 1965), un ragtime para marchar que culpa a generales, a Wall Street y a los padres crédulos, no a los soldados. Phil Ochs ironizó con «Draft Dodger Rag». En enero de 1966 Ronald Reagan hizo de los disturbios de Berkeley, «un carnaval de pesadilla», el eje de su campaña a gobernador.

refs.q: Energised by the Free Speech Movement, student activists began to turn from civil rights to Vietnam.
refs.para: Energised by the Free Speech Movement, student activists began to turn from civil rights to Vietnam. In May 1965, the Vietnam Day Committee (VDC) – founded by Jerry Rubin and Abbie Hoffman, among others – was formed to expand the peace movement and raise public awareness of the war by civil disobedience and community action. In August, with slogans like ‘Make Love Not War’, activists from the VDC picketed troop trains carrying soldiers from the nearby Oakland Army Base who were bound for Vietnam.
refs.chapter: Marzo: The Ballad of the Green Berets: la guerra de Vietnam en Estados Unidos

refs.q: Out of this ferment came one of the most pointed musical protests against the war.
refs.para: Out of this ferment came one of the most pointed musical protests against the war. Released in October 1965 on the Berkeley Rag Baby label, ‘I Feel Like I’m Fixin’ to Die Rag’ begins with the sound of gunfire before Country Joe McDonald offers the invitation: ‘Well, come on, all of you big strong men / Uncle Sam needs your help again.’ Over four blackly humorous verses, McDonald apportions blame for Vietnam, castigating generals, Wall Street and unthinking parents who buy the propaganda.
